title: One of the most reproduced photos ever was taken 29,000 km away

cover.alt: The whole Earth, fully lit, showing Africa, Arabia and the Antarctic ice under swirling clouds.

body: On 7 December 1972, on the way to the Moon, an Apollo 17 astronaut photographed the entire sunlit face of Earth from about **29,400 km** away. A cropped, rotated version, known as *The Blue Marble*, became one of the most reproduced images in history.

slides.label: between Apollo 17 and Earth’s surface
slides.text: Far enough to fit the whole planet in one frame of a 70 mm Hasselblad camera.

slides.heading: Why it’s fully lit
slides.text: The Sun was behind the spacecraft, so the crew saw Earth as a full disc. Most photos from space show it partly in shadow.

slides.question: In what year did a camera first photograph Earth from space?
slides.explanation: 1946, eleven years before Sputnik: on 24 October a camera on a captured German V-2 rocket took the first photos of Earth from space, about 105 km up.

slides.heading: Earliest first
items: First photo of Earth from a V-2 rocket
slides.explanation: 1946: a captured V-2 rocket. 1968: Apollo 8’s Earthrise. 1972: Apollo 17’s The Blue Marble. 1990: Voyager 1’s Pale Blue Dot, from about 6 billion km away.

events.text: A camera on a captured V-2 rocket takes the first photos of Earth from space, about 105 km up.
Apollo 8’s *Earthrise* shows Earth rising over the Moon.
Voyager 1 shows Earth as a *Pale Blue Dot*, about 6 billion km away.

slides.heading: How far away the camera was
slides.note: Voyager 1’s Pale Blue Dot, from about 6 billion km, would need a bar 200,000 times longer

slides.text: Look again at that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us.
